lesson.title: Nacht & Licht: the gh→ch Inversion
lesson.subtitle: The English gh words that German kept sounding — and thought↔dachte's payoff

hook.title: The Night the Letters Died
hook.content: English 'night' is a crime scene. The gh-letters are the victim: they were once a real, throaty [x] — and German still pronounces them every single night: Nacht. The full lineup of the deceased: light/Licht, eight/acht, right/Recht, might/Macht, laugh/lachen, daughter/Tochter. English spelled the funeral and kept the corpse in writing; German never got the memo and still sounds every one. And the crossover star: thought ↔ dachte — th→d, gh→ch, the whole ghost alphabet in one word pair.

footnotes.title: laugh's Strange Afterlife
footnotes.content: Most gh words went silent (night, daughter); 'laugh' did something stranger — it turned gh into an F sound. German lachen kept the original [x]. So English 'laugh' is a mispronunciation of lachen that got a spelling pension.

pattern.title: Sound the Ghosts
pattern.content: The night row: night ↔ Nacht, light ↔ Licht. The number row: eight ↔ acht, right ↔ Recht (Du hast recht — you are right). The might row: might ↔ Macht (Wissen ist Macht — knowledge is power). The servile row: knight ↔ Knecht — in English the servant became a nobleman; in German the Knecht stayed a farmhand. The freight row: freight ↔ Fracht (cargo). And the crown: think/thought ↔ denken/dachte — the double shift you can now fully decode: th→d, gh→ch, vowel included.
pattern.linguist_note: The gh→ch correspondence is your ninth and final Atlas family. With it, the decode engine is complete: PF-, TH-, T-, K-, D-, V-, GH-, Y-, and the ablaut melodies — every Germanic consonant correspondence accounted for.

exercises.prompt: Sound the ghosts — match the silent-gh words with their ch twins:
exercises.explanation: Every silent gh in English is a sounding ch in German — the ghost letters were never empty.

exercises.prompt: The crown jewel: which shifts decode 'thought' into 'dachte'?
options: TH → D and gh → ch (plus the vowel drift)
exercises.target_answer: TH → D and gh → ch (plus the vowel drift)
exercises.explanation: The dental hardening and the guttural survival — two laws, one irregular past, fully decoded.

exercises.prompt: 'Knight' and 'Knecht' — why did the meanings drift apart?
options: In English the servant rose to nobility; in German the Knecht stayed a farmhand
Knight means farmhand in modern English too
exercises.target_answer: In English the servant rose to nobility; in German the Knecht stayed a farmhand
exercises.meaning: knight ↔ Knecht: one word, two social fates
exercises.explanation: Same word, same gh→ch, opposite class journeys — the word history of two feudal systems. The night sky keeps the theme: der Mond (moon), der Stern (star) — Mond is moon's own twin, Stern is star with the -en tail.

exercises.prompt: What English word is the twin of 'Macht'?
exercises.explanation: 'Might is right' and 'Wissen ist Macht' — the same word about power, both still sounding their guttural.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Good night! I think of you'
exercises.target_answer: Gute Nacht ich denke an dich
exercises.meaning: Good night! I think of you
exercises.explanation: Nacht (gh→ch) and denke (th→d) — the two ghost-laws in one bedtime sentence. Und das Licht ist hell — bright — the gh→ch word for the light itself.

summary.outcome: Sound every English gh as German ch and decode thought/dachte completely.

use_example.german: Gute Nacht — ich denke an dich.
use_example.english: Good night — I think of you.

summary.takeaway: Nacht, Licht, acht, Recht, Macht — the gh never died in German. thought ↔ dachte crowns the map.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Tochter's double-shift showdown and the sagen/gestern y→g twins — the last Atlas lessons.

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

knecht.context_phrase: Der Knecht arbeitet auf dem Hof.
knecht.context_translation: The farmhand works on the estate.
knecht.etymology_derivation: gh → ch (knight ↔ Knecht). In English it elevated to noble warrior; in German it remained farm servant.

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

hell.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *halliz 'resounding'; English bright/light is not cognate — hell is akin to English hall. [wiktionary]

mond.context_phrase: Der Mond ist heute Nacht hell.
mond.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *mānō — the same ancient moon-word as English moon. [wiktionary]

stern.context_phrase: Ich sehe einen Stern am Himmel.
stern.context_translation: I see a star in the sky.
stern.etymology_derivation: Old High German sterno — cognate with English star. [wiktionary]

voll.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fullaz — English full is the explicit cognate. [wiktionary]

nass.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *nat — cognate with Dutch nat; English wet is a translation match, not a cognate. [wiktionary]

selbst.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *selbaz; the page lists English self as the direct cognate — the f closing to b in German plus an excrescent t. [wiktionary]

muttersprache.etymology_derivation: Mutter + Sprache, mother language; a loan translation of Latin lingua materna, the same mother-language metaphor as English mother tongue. [wiktionary]

anders.context_translation: In Germany many things are different.
anders.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *anþeraz (documented on the page); the High German d is the shifted th of English other, the same dental hardening as think and denken. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
